subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: The repolarisation phase of an action potential is brought about by:
options: The sodium-potassium pump alone
Potassium channels opening so K+ diffuses out of the axon
Calcium ions entering the axon
Sodium channels opening
questions.explain: Voltage-gated K+ channels open and K+ leaves the axon, restoring the negative internal potential (repolarisation).

questions.q: In the cohesion-tension theory of water transport, water moves up the xylem because:
options: Active transport pumps water from root to leaf
Osmosis pushes water from the leaves down to the roots
Transpiration creates tension, and cohesion between water molecules pulls a continuous column upward
Root pressure alone is sufficient in tall trees
questions.explain: Evaporation from leaves lowers pressure, and hydrogen-bonded cohesion lets a continuous water column be pulled up under tension.

questions.q: Ultrafiltration in the renal glomerulus occurs because:
options: Active transport pushes plasma into the Bowman's capsule
The afferent arteriole is wider than the efferent arteriole, lowering pressure
High hydrostatic blood pressure forces small molecules through the basement membrane, which acts as a filter
Plasma proteins are actively secreted into the filtrate
questions.explain: High pressure (helped by a narrower efferent arteriole) forces water and small solutes through the basement membrane, which holds back proteins and cells.

questions.q: Herd immunity protects unvaccinated individuals because:
options: The pathogen mutates to become harmless
A high proportion of immune people reduces the chance of an unvaccinated person meeting an infected person
Antibodies are passed between people on contact
Vaccines spread immunity through the air
questions.explain: When enough of the population is immune, transmission is interrupted, so susceptible individuals are unlikely to encounter the pathogen.

The movement of Cl- into red blood cells to balance the charge as HCO3- leaves
The exchange of oxygen for chloride at the alveoli
The loss of Cl- from plasma during digestion
questions.explain: As hydrogencarbonate ions diffuse out of red cells, chloride ions move in to maintain electrical neutrality.

questions.q: An antigen is best defined as:
options: A molecule (usually protein) that is recognised as foreign and triggers an immune response
A protein that always causes disease
An antibody produced by plasma cells
A toxin released by bacteria
questions.explain: Antigens are molecules, often surface proteins, identified as non-self and capable of stimulating an immune response.

questions.q: In a pregnancy test, monoclonal antibodies are used to:
options: Destroy the hCG hormone
Convert hCG into a dye
Produce hCG in the urine
Bind specifically to the hCG hormone, giving a coloured line when present
questions.explain: Mobile antibodies bind hCG and are then trapped by immobilised antibodies in the test window, producing a visible coloured line.

questions.q: Glucose is absorbed across the ileum epithelium into the blood by:
options: Co-transport with sodium ions, the Na+ gradient being maintained by a sodium-potassium pump
Active transport directly using ATP at the apical membrane
Facilitated diffusion at the apical membrane independent of sodium
Simple diffusion only, down its concentration gradient
questions.explain: Na+/glucose co-transporters move glucose against its gradient using the Na+ gradient set up by the Na+/K+ pump on the basal membrane.

questions.q: During inspiration in a mammal, the pressure in the thorax falls because:
options: The external intercostal muscles relax
The volume of the thoracic cavity increases as the diaphragm flattens and the ribs move up and out
The diaphragm relaxes and domes upward
Surfactant reduces the surface tension of the alveoli
questions.explain: Contraction of the diaphragm and external intercostals increases thoracic volume, lowering pressure below atmospheric so air flows in.

questions.q: Insects limit water loss from their tracheal system mainly by:
options: Increasing ventilation by abdominal pumping
Closing the spiracles using valves and hairs
Producing surfactant in the tracheoles
Using haemoglobin to carry oxygen in the blood
questions.explain: Spiracles can be closed by valves, reducing the evaporative water loss that would otherwise occur from the moist tracheal lining.

questions.q: The secondary immune response is faster and stronger than the primary because:
options: Phagocytosis no longer occurs
Antigens are weaker on second exposure
The pathogen has fewer antigens
Memory cells rapidly divide and differentiate into plasma cells, producing antibodies quickly
questions.explain: Memory cells formed during the primary response allow a rapid proliferation of plasma cells and a higher, quicker antibody output.

questions.q: In the sliding filament theory, muscle contraction shortens the sarcomere because:
options: The H zone widens as filaments slide apart
Calcium ions are pumped out of the sarcoplasm
The actin and myosin filaments themselves shorten
Myosin heads form cross-bridges and pull the actin filaments past the myosin toward the centre
questions.explain: Myosin heads bind actin and, powered by ATP, pull the thin filaments inward so the sarcomere shortens while filament lengths stay the same.
